newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mulls more direct role in liver transplants.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mulls more direct role in liver transplants.

text.p: Stepping into one of the most contentious issues in medical ethics, the government opened hearings Tuesday on whether it should play a more direct role in deciding how to allocate livers for transplants.

The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) began three days of hearings involving patients, surgeons, hospital officals, organ donor groups and medical economists in a bid to find the best system for distributing livers.
Livers for transplants are in short supply, with about 4,000 available each year for 7,000 people who are waiting. Last year, 800 people died while waiting for a new liver.

"In recent years, the debate around the allocation system for livers has been the most vexing and controversial issue confronting the transplant community," HHS Assistant Secretary Dr. Philip Lee said in opening the hearings.
A key issue is whether there should be a national waiting list or if organs should be assigned through the regional system introduced five years ago.

HHS will probably decide early next year whether or how to intervene in the policies now set by the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS), a nonprofit agency based in Richmond, Va., which has a federal contract for overseeing many aspects of national organ donation and transplant policy.
Twenty-seven members of Congress urged HHS Secretary Donna Shalala Tuesday not to get involved. "We strongly caution against usurping UNOS' traditional role," they wrote.
Critics say the regional system means vast inequities, with people in some states waiting days or weeks for a new liver while sicker people elsewhere may wait a year or more.

"The system does not treat patients fairly," said University of Pittsburgh transplant surgeon Dr. John Fung, a leading advocate of a national system that he said would in itself resolve many of the other thorny allocation problems.

Other difficult questions involve whether to give priority to the chronically ill or to those with acute liver failure, whether to favour a few big national transplant centres like Pittsburgh or continue the recent trend of encouraging more smaller regional centres, and whether the government should have a more direct role in setting transplant policies that involve public funding and affect public health.
Money also plays a role. Liver transplants are big business. Small centres want to get a piece of the market and the large established ones want to keep their share.
UNOS recently announced that starting Jan. 20 patients who suffered acute sudden liver failure would go to the top of the waiting list, ahead of seriously ill chronic patients.

"The number of acute liver patients is small and the difference in the rules will have minimal impact on the uncertainties facing those who wait," said UNOS president Dr. James Burdick, a transplant surgeon at Johns Hopkins.
Critics, and patient advocates, say that will make it hard for the chronically ill ever to get transplants.

"I want the sickest person to have the first opportunity, even if it's not me," said Robert Beideler, a 52-year-old who contracted hepatitis through a blood transfusion. "But I want everybody to have an equal opportunity, and for the chronically ill this policy puts our lives in danger."

Modifying that controversial change, UNOS said Tuesday it was working on a way of identifying those chronically ill people who should be a higher priority if they experienced "true, acute" deterioration -- what surgeons call "crashing."
UNOS said transplant centres and surgeons overwhelmingly support it, and oppose a greater government role. But other witnesses shared Fung's critical view.
Dr. Charles Miller of New York's Mount Sinai Medical Centre said UNOS's allocation system allows some people to get transplants before they needed them while others died waiting.
